articles.title: ‘The Vow’ star Jace Cates recommits to saving himself for marriage despite ‘sex-positive culture’
articles.summary: "Chris Harrison’s: The Vow" star Jace Cates opens up about saving himself for marriage, why faith in relationships matters, and dating in a sex-positive culture.
articles.body: "Chris Harrison's: The Vow" star, Jace Cates, is giving his opinion on modern dating and how the current "sex-positive culture" can complicate things. During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 30-year-old reality star said he is committed to saving himself for marriage, noting that while he was in his 20s, "there were times that I absolutely" wasn't in "lockstep with my faith," noting that might be why he was "single at 30." "I talk about being a fan of Jesus or also being a follower of Jesus. There's a big difference," he said. "So, when you're a follower of Jesus, there is specific beliefs that you have to actually be a follower of Jesus to build that relationship around Jesus and have faith be a part of the relationship. And the next person I'm intimate with, I want that to be my wife. And I think that's important." Adding: "And I know it's hard, because it's a very sex-positive culture. And it's a sacrifice for sure for people to make. And I think that's something that people have to navigate." CHRIS HARRISON RETURNS TO REALITY TV WITH 'THE VOW,' FOX NATION'S FIRST-EVER DATING SHOW "I think we got away from being okay with talking about faith in a relationship and going to church together," he said. "And I think as people are looking intentionally and leading with faith, those are conversations that couples need to have sooner rather than later. That's about intentional dating and I think it's something that people need to discuss." WATCH HERE: ‘CHRIS HARRISON’S: THE VOW'S' JACE CATES WANTS THE NEXT PERSON HE IS INTIMATE WITH TO BE HIS WIFE The new Fox Nation show, "Chris Harrison's: The Vow," follows Cates as he navigates relationships with 10 women seeking lasting commitment and marriage over six episodes. His experience on the show ultimately changed his view on dating, as he was left completely unplugged as he "was away from my phone, my laptop [and] couldn't communicate with my family." And it's something I've tried to take back to my real life," he explained. "One thing I'll say, viewers, when they tune into the show and see what happens, I'm just extremely grateful that I had this experience to show me how important that is more than I even believed before I went on the show." In addition to the "sex-positive culture," Cates thinks technology is also a problem when it comes to modern dating, as "people have access to people now, more than ever," noting this is when being intentional in the pursuit of love is important. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Cates told Fox News Digital, that the faith aspect of the show separates it from others of its kind, noting everyone who participated was "trying to build something real and people actually looking for love." When it comes to what he is looking for in a relationship, the Oregon native admitted he is hoping for a more traditional marriage, but not in the way people might think, noting the term has a "negative connotation right now." "I think for me, traditional marriage means just supporting your person 100 percent in what they are looking to do in life," he said. "And if my future wife wants to be a stay-at-home mom, I want to be a supportive husband and support her 100 percent. If she wants to be a CEO of a company, I will support her 100 percent and we will make it work. I think that is what traditional means to me. articles.title: British police name suspects charged in break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate's home
articles.summary: Two men are charged after a break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate's Anmer Hall on the Sandringham Estate, with police deploying dogs and drones.
articles.body: British police announced on Wednesday two men have been charged following a report of a break-in at Prince William and Princess Kate’s country home on the Sandringham Estate. The Norfolk Constabulary confirmed that Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were arrested in connection with the incident at Anmer Hall; authorities said the property was unoccupied at the time. The men have been charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. They remain in custody and are due to appear in Norwich Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday. The suspects were taken into custody near the country house after police received a call about suspicious activity at around 6 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET) on Monday. FORMER PRINCE ANDREW ‘SHAKEN’ BY MASKED MAN THREAT, BUT MORE SECURITY WOULD SPARK ‘PUBLIC BACKLASH’: EXPERT "Officers attended and specialist resources, including police dogs, drones and the National Police Air Service helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches in the area," police said in a statement to Fox News. The Sun reported that William, Kate, and their three children — Prince George, Princess Charlotte, and Prince Louis — were staying at their primary residence, Forest Lodge in Windsor, at the time of the incident. Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom residence on the 20,000-acre Sandringham Estate, was given to William and Kate as a wedding gift by the late Queen Elizabeth II. Prior to moving in, the couple oversaw a £1.5 million renovation that included major security upgrades, such as rerouting a public road, planting dense tree lines for privacy and establishing a seasonal no-fly zone over the property. RENTALS NOW ALLOWED IN HISTORIC WATER TOWER ON KING CHARLES' SANDRINGHAM ESTATE WHERE ROYALS SPEND CHRISTMAS The family regularly visits the country estate for weekend getaways and school holidays, and it served as a private sanctuary for Kate during her cancer treatment in 2024. The break-in raises fresh concerns over royal security, as William and his immediate family receive 24-hour armed protection as working royals. The incident also marks the latest security scare on royal grounds. articles.title: Country music star Darius Rucker reveals facing racism from Black fans over genre switch
articles.summary: Darius Rucker revealed on "The BobbyCast" Tuesday that racism from Black critics, not just White people, has crushed him since his country music switch.
articles.body: Former Hootie & the Blowfish lead vocalist Darius Rucker revealed Tuesday that he faced racism by Black people once he switched to country music. Rucker remarked on Netflix's "The BobbyCast" that in the years since switching to the country genre, he has hardly received recognition for being the first Black man since Charley Pride in 1983 to have a No. 1 hit on the Hot Country Songs chart. He said that this dismissal of his success unexpectedly came from both racist White people and Black critics. "I'm not talking about just White folks being racist. I'm talking about like Black folks going, 'What the f--- are you doing, man, really?'" Rucker said. DARIUS RUCKER SAYS HE USED TO DRINK A BOTTLE OF WHISKEY A DAY DURING WILD HOOTIE & THE BLOWFISH YEARS Rucker recalled a recent incident of a Black woman confronting him over his race in a public restaurant. "The other night, some woman comes on and says, 'You know you're Black, right?' And I just went off, and I was like, 'I've been doing this for 60 years. You think these White motherf---ers haven't told me my whole life I'm Black? I f---ing know I'm Black,’" he said. Rucker also recounted meeting with Pride before his death, who remarked that despite being the first Black performer to win the Entertainer of the Year award at the Country Music Association Awards, he was never invited to be on the cover of Black-centered magazines like Ebony or Jet. MEDIA'S OUTRAGE AT LUKE COMBS COVERING TRACY CHAPMAN'S 'FAST CAR' UNDERSCORES OBSESSION WITH RACE: CRITICS "I thought me and you did what people say we can't do, not shouldn't do, we can't do … and we did that and instead of embracing us for one second and saying, ‘Look what these two brothers did,’ [they] just ignore us," Rucker said. He acknowledged that he would likely never win over these Black critics but admitted that the "hate" he's received from Black people still hurts. "It hurts more because the White side I expected. I know it's coming. I was born in Charleston, South Carolina. I know that's coming, and I'm ready to deal with that. But when it comes from the Black side, it crushes you. It crushes your soul," Rucker said. DARIUS RUCKER IS 'SO AGAINST' HIS KIDS BECOMING MUSICIANS LIKE HIM DESPITE THEIR INTEREST In a comment to Fox News Digital, Project 21 Black Leadership Ambassador Phil Bell said that Rucker's experience with the Black community is not unique to him, calling it discrimination that denigrates individual success. articles.title: ‘It’s not for the timid’: Blade Runner 2099’s showrunner on adapting the series for TV
articles.summary: Blade Runner 2099 showrunner Silka Luisa talks about her approach to adapting the cyberpunk classic into a streaming series on Amazon Prime Video.
articles.body: As a longtime fan of the films, Blade Runner 2099 showrunner Silka Luisa says she was more excited than scared when it came to adapting the series for TV. The new show is set 50 years after the 2017 film Blade Runner 2049 and imagines a bleak future where artificial humans known as replicants have taken over society after a brutal war. Luisa, who previously served as showrunner on Apple TV’s Shining Girls adaptation, says she largely had to put any concerns about the monumental task of following up Blade Runner out of her mind while working on the show. “I just don’t think you can approach Blade Runner with fear,” she tells The Verge. “It’s a bold concept. It always has been. P.K. Dick took really big swings and it’s not for the timid. So any fears I had I just ignored and kept focused on the monumental task at hand.” And yet, there was one particular moment during production that made Luisa pause and think about just how big of a deal this project was. Blade Runner 2099 stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer as pair of noir detectives — Yeoh is a replicant approaching the end of her life, while Schafer is trying to hide the fact that she’s human — and, in the grand tradition of previous leads Harrison Ford and Ryan Gosling, each has a distinct and iconic jacket. “Once they put the coats on, it really did just transform them,” Luisa says. “The screen test was one of the few moments where I stopped myself and was just blown away by the fact that I was making Blade Runner.” Blade Runner 2099 is streaming on Amazon Prime Video today, and you can read my chat with Luisa exploring everything from the show’s origins to the research process to those all-important jackets. The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. [Image: What do you think it is about Blade Runner that has made it so enduring? It’s one of the rare properties that asks really deep philosophical questions, but within a detective noir narrative. I think it’s the juxtaposition of both a structure that’s accessible and familiar, but then these really heady, vital questions: What does it mean to be human? How do you find connection? Just these evergreen concepts that every generation needs to grapple with in their own way and in their own time. There really isn’t anything else like Blade Runner. Given all of that, was it intimidating or scary to take this on? I know it seems insane almost to say no, but I just don’t think you can approach Blade Runner with fear. It’s a bold concept. It always has been. P.K. Dick took really big swings and it’s not for the timid. So any fears I had I just ignored and kept focused on the monumental task at hand. And you just stay so concentrated on moving the show forward at each step that you’re not really thinking of it in that objective sense. Does the time gap in the narrative help with that and give you the space to create your own thing? Absolutely. Every iteration has evolved forward. [Original Blade Runner director Ridley Scott] took a big leap from the book. There definitely are touchstones from the novel in his film, but he put his own stamp on that story. And [Blade Runner 2049 director Denis Villeneuve], it’s the same thing. 2049 is mesmerizing, it’s spectacular, but in its own way. It feels like it sits in the world of the Blade Runner canon, but is not a replica of what Ridley did. And that’s what makes it so special. That actually gave us a lot of freedom to try and carve our own path, because if the world is too familiar, it’s not unsettling and it’s not going to give you any feeling of awe. You’ve already seen it before. And so you have to make it your own in some sense. So where did you start with this story? What was the initial concept? The starting point was the idea of technology overtaking us. The war between “robots” and humans is something that has been visited in science fiction many times. And to me what felt fresh wasn’t necessarily what the war looked like, but what the aftermath looked like. I couldn’t close my eyes and picture off the top of my head what would happen to us, what would society shift into, what is post-human. That was really exciting. So it definitely started with the concept of this junction point between the world as we know it and a possible world to come. [Image: Was the idea of having this inverse relationship from the original film, where replicants are now hunting humans, always part of the concept? Yes, it started with the idea of flipping the world, and once you do that at the macro level, you start to think about what is the more intimate story you’re telling. And if you flip the world now suddenly you have a replicant society, it’s not about a replicant trying to look human, it’s the opposite way around. And so an undercover story just seemed like a natural answer to what would be the narrative shape. It also gave me a relationship as opposed to a single person’s journey. Was it a lot of work imagining what this new replicant society would be like? So much of the initial writing process was just the visuals. It was really hard to write in spaces that I couldn’t picture. We started to put images up in the writers room from the real world, a blend of films, unusual references from the real world, historical references. You have to ask: What does the texture of the space feel like? Who works there? How long has it existed? What neighborhood is it in? You start to ask all of these questions, and you need to know the answers to write the scenes. It definitely slows the process of writing. Because normally I love to do a lot of historical research. If I’m setting something in a place, I would read a lot about it, and find all of the details in the real world. Here I needed that same amount of detail, but we had to create it. The Blade Runner films have such a slow and deliberate pacing. How do you think about that when you’re doing a story that’s eight hours long compared to a much shorter movie? The pacing of the show was one of the biggest conversation points early on, because everybody would be wary of having a truly Blade Runner pace. When you’re in a theater, it is such a meditative experience to be in that world. And there was a fear that if you translate it to television, people won’t have the patience for that. So on the page, I really was pushing the momentum of the storytelling, to the point of even not having exteriors, where you’re just jumping into scenes. In the editing process, once we started to actually look at cuts, if you cut it too tightly you don’t have these moments of breath where the music can live. Once we had [composer Leopold Ross’] score, and we started putting it to pictures, you want to give him a moment in the sun. You want to have those dreamier sections of the show that are, to me, really fundamental to what makes something Blade Runner. It’s always a question of how far you can stretch the rubber band. Everyone will debate whether the pacing is too slow or too fast, and it’s a really hard calibration. Blade Runner has such a strong lineage of cool jackets. How important was it to get that look right for both Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer? Our costume designer Helen [Huang] is phenomenal. Her jackets are incredible, and I love that both of them have really distinct silhouettes. Helen is so thoughtful in how she starts to conceive of these really iconic pieces. For Michelle, she wanted to have something that was referencing a more traditional trench, and then for Hunter it was more of a bomber jacket. She pulled all of these incredible historical references and then blended them with different textures that would make sense with the harsh environment. It’s just masterful work. Once they put the coats on, it really did just transform them. The screen test was one of the few moments where I stopped myself and was just blown away by the fact that I was making Blade Runner.

articles.title: Five Mexicans arrested in Nigeria over $227m meth lab
articles.summary: This is the fourth industrial-scale meth laboratory with alleged links to Mexican drug cartels to have been discovered in Nigeria in recent months.
articles.body:
Five Mexican nationals and a Nigerian businessman have been arrested in Nigeria after authorities uncovered an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory, the country's drug enforcement agency says.

More than 1.5 tonnes of the highly addictive synthetic drug, commonly known as meth, was seized from the facility in the south-eastern state of Enugu. The haul included both finished drugs and meth still being produced.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) estimates the drugs are worth $227m (£173m).

It is the fourth industrial-scale meth laboratory with alleged links to Mexican drug cartels to have been discovered in Nigeria in recent months.

The Nigerian businessman, 63-year-old Chuks Enoch Ezeike, also known as "Over Size", is accused of setting up the laboratory and smuggling the five Mexicans into the country using forged Argentine, Colombian and Chilean passports.

The NDLEA identified the five as Oscar Ramos-Cardenas, who it described as the alleged leader of the group, Juan Antonio Sarabia-Cabrera, Luis Enrique Garcia-Amador, Jose Alejandro Renteria-Reyes and Salomon Cabanillas-Torres.

The laboratory, situated behind an oil company in Enugu, also had accommodation for the Mexican nationals, allowing them to live and work there without attracting attention, the agency said.

Speaking at a news conference in the capital, Abuja, on Wednesday, NDLEA chief Mohamed Buba Marwa said the arrests followed a seven-month investigation involving several countries.

The agency had been monitoring Ezeike since April, when it received intelligence allegedly linking him to Ramos-Cardenas, a Mexican national suspected of specialising in large-scale meth production.

In August, the five Mexicans were refused entry into Nigeria after arriving at Abuja's international airport and were sent back to Mexico.

But less than a month later, they tried again, travelling through Colombia and France before arriving in neighbouring Benin, where they were allegedly given forged passports.

This time, Nigerian authorities deliberately allowed them into the country, Marwa said.

"We wanted the whole network: the meth specialist, the financier, the factory and the product. Sending them home a second time would only have postponed the problem," he said.

The men were allegedly met by Ezeike in Lagos before being taken to Enugu, where they were kept under surveillance.

More than 200 anti-narcotics officers were deployed on 11 November to raid the laboratory and a hotel where Ezeike was staying in simultaneous operations.

The five Mexicans were arrested while producing the drug, the agency said. Ezeike told investigators they had been due to leave Nigeria two days later.

Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals used to manufacture meth, as well as industrial equipment, were also seized.

The NDLEA said Ezeike had admitted owning the laboratory and bringing the Mexican nationals into Nigeria to produce the drug.

Investigators believe the operation was part of a wider international criminal network in which a Mexican cartel recruited and paid specialists to manufacture meth, while Nigerian collaborators allegedly provided the facilities and resources.

The agency has not identified the Mexican cartel it suspects was involved or said whether the six suspects have been formally charged.

The arrests come amid growing concerns about Mexican drug cartels setting up production bases in West Africa, a region long used as a transit route for illicit drugs.

While some of the meth produced in the region supplies a growing local market, traffickers also target lucrative overseas markets, particularly in Europe and Asia.

Earlier this year, Nigerian authorities uncovered similar laboratories in Ogun, Oyo and Ebonyi states.

The latest operation brings to 10 the number of suspected Mexican meth production specialists arrested in Nigeria in recent months, according to the NDLEA. Five others arrested in earlier operations are already in custody awaiting trial.

Issuing a warning to foreign drug cartels, Marwa said: "Nigeria is not your laboratory. It is not your warehouse, and it is not your transit route."

articles.title: New Miss Universe’s Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win
articles.summary: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers.”
articles.body: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers.” Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe. “It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement. The town of some 39,000 people is named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers could barely contain itself. “La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win. “So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.” Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the U.S. Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviors. She is the sixth Puerto Rican woman to win the Miss Universe crown, ending a 20-year wait for the island. Thunderous applause greeted Barreto at Puerto Rico’s José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum each time she advanced through the final of the competition. Her hands flew to her face in shock as she was announced Miss Universe 2026. Minutes later, she shimmied her hips as she took a victory lap to ABBA’s “Dancing Queen.” And thousands of Puerto Ricans across the U.S. territory danced with her. “It’s a truly spectacular achievement,” San Sebastián Mayor Eladio Cardona Quiles told The Associated Press. “All the most beautiful women in the universe are there, and she managed to stand out. I’m happy she represented ‘los pepinianos.’” Cardona attended the pageant, while fans gathered in San Sebastián’s public plaza to watch on a big screen. Afterward, they formed a caravan, honking their horns into the night to celebrate Barreto’s victory.

articles.title: ‘Friday Night Lights,’ ‘Mosquito Bowl’ author says America has lost the Greatest Generation's sense of duty
articles.summary: "The Mosquito Bowl" author Buzz Bissinger says America has forgotten the selfless duty of the Greatest Generation, whose college football stars left fame behind to fight in WWII.
articles.body: "Friday Night Lights" author Buzz Bissinger believes modern America has lost touch with the selflessness that once defined the "Greatest Generation." The 72-year-old Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist penned the 2022 nonfiction book "The Mosquito Bowl," which was adapted into Peter Berg's new Netflix war movie of the same name. "The Mosquito Bowl" tells the true story of elite college football stars who walked away from fame and future wealth to enlist in the Marines and fight in the Pacific Theater during World War II. While speaking with Fox News Digital at the film's premiere during the AFI Film Festival, Bissinger argued that kind of sacrifice has largely disappeared today. HOLLYWOOD MARINE VETERAN ROB RIGGLE DOUBTS MODERN STARS WOULD MAKE JIMMY STEWART'S WWII SACRIFICE "I think we've forgotten," Bissinger said. "I know they're called the Greatest Generation, but we have forgotten what it is like to serve, to have a sense of duty, to do something regardless of whether you're going to come back or not. And these are things we have to remember." "We were together," he continued. "These men fought. They were never heroes. They never thought of themselves as heroes. They were ordinary men in extraordinary circumstances who felt it was really, really important to serve their country. And many of them didn't come back." AMERICA'S VETERANS AND MILITARY HEROES DESERVE FAR MORE RECOGNITION THAN THEY GET: YOUTUBE STAR "And they need to be memorialized," he added. "It helps remind me of the greatness of this country, just how great this country was. There was no division. We were in unison, and these men personified that. And they had great lives ahead of them, but they didn't make it." Both the book and the movie depict the Mosquito Bowl, a tackle football game played on Christmas Eve in 1944 on Guadalcanal between two Marine regiments whose ranks included some of the country's top former college football players. Months later, 15 of the 65 players were killed fighting in the Battle of Okinawa. WATCH: 'Friday Night Lights' author Buzz Bissinger says America has 'forgotten' the Greatest Generation's duty FOX SPORTS TO HONOR MILITARY AHEAD OF VETERANS DAY WITH TWO-DAY SALUTE DURING COLLEGE FOOTBALL, NFL COVERAGE During his interview with Fox News Digital, Bissinger drew a comparison between modern celebrity sports culture and the dozens of elite college athletes who put their lives on the line in World War II, many of whom had already been drafted by NFL teams. "I was actually thinking about how many pro football players have served in the military. The answer is virtually none," he said. "To have 65 football players who went to college and are now in the Marine Corps serving, forget it." KELSEY GRAMMER STILL FEELS 'SENSE OF SMALLNESS' FOR NOT SERVING IN MILITARY: 'I DO MY BEST TO MAKE UP FOR IT' "It was a whole different era," Bissinger continued. "You gave up your dreams. You had no choice. You had to serve. It was in your heart." He cited Dave Schreiner, a celebrated University of Wisconsin two-time All-American football star who turned down an NFL career and non-combat military posts to enlist in the U.S. Marine Corps and serve on the front lines. Schreiner was mortally wounded during the Battle of Okinawa in June 1945 and died the following day at age 24. LAST SURVIVING 'ROSIE THE RIVETERS' HONORED BY WWII MUSEUM ON D-DAY ANNIVERSARY: 'WE CAN DO IT' "All of them could have gotten out, I think, because they were athletes, and athletes are coveted," Bissinger said. "But they didn't. They didn't. It was offered, and they said, ‘No, I have to go. I have to go.’ And that's pretty rare. You will not see that happen today." Bissinger pointed out that many of the football players who fought in WWII could have used their status to get safer stateside opportunities but refused. THE DAY AFTER MEMORIAL DAY, AMERICA’S DEBT TO THE FALLEN STILL REMAINS Berg's adaptation of "The Mosquito Bowl" focuses on four real-life college football stars who enlisted in the Marines after Pearl Harbor, including Schreiner, who was played by Broadway star Tom Francis, John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård) and Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson). The screenplay was co-written by Berg and Mark L Smith. PETER BERG SAYS 'CALL OF DUTY' MOVIE WILL EXPLORE 'THE COST OF WAR' WITH SERIOUS TONE Bissinger spent five years researching and writing "The Mosquito Bowl" including digging through military records and family archives. While speaking with Fox News Digital, the author compared the process to a "detective story" since many of the first-hand witnesses and people who participated in the real-life Mosquito Bowl had died. During his research, Bissinger made a personal discovery when he unexpectedly uncovered his own late father's service in the 4th Marine Regiment. "He never talked about it. I didn't know, was he on the line? Was he a rifleman? Was he, you know, a waiter?" Bissinger recalled. Bissinger, who was born Harry Gerard Bissinger III, explained that he was searching for his own name in the records since he was named after his father. "So I looked up the roster records, and his name is my name," Bissinger said. "I'm the third, he's the second. And there's his name. But not only that, he is a rifleman, so he's on the lines. And he's in the 4th Regiment, which is one of the regiments that I was writing about, so I'm seeing all these names from the book and, for all I know, he could have been there. He could have been at the game." "It was mind-blowing, and it put me over the top," he continued. "And what I learned — I'm so proud of him. And I stop because I get worked up. I just wish I could have said that 'I'm really proud of you. I'm really, really proud of you.' But he's been gone for a long time." However, Bissinger told Fox News Digital that learning about his father's history established a connection that they didn't have when he was alive. "I've never felt closer to him," Bissinger said. Berg's late father, Laurence Berg, was also a Marine who served in the Korean War. Bissinger recalled he and the director, who are also second cousins, recently shared a moment in which they wondered how their fathers would have reacted to "The Mosquito Bowl." "Last week, we were walking out of the Marine Corps Museum, and we both said, ‘What would it be like if our fathers were here?,'" Bissinger said. "Now, they were kind of critical guys, so the first thing they would do is criticize the film, but then they would hug us, and they would feel such incredible pride, not just for us, but for the family," he continued. "It would have been a great moment, but we'll have to imagine it." Bissinger said that while audiences remain hungry for stories about real-life heroes like his father and the men of the Mosquito Bowl, he believes Hollywood too often waters down the true cost of combat. "I think what happens is, particularly in war movies, they ultimately get sanitized," he said. "Filmmakers, directors, studios are afraid of showing war as it is because they think people can't handle it. I think that's ridiculous, and I think it's wrong." "In order for us to see just how tragic and brutal war is, we have to see it," Bissinger continued. "We have to see it. I tried to do that in the book and Pete has certainly done that in the film. People may flinch, people may not be able to handle it, but to me, it doesn't matter. If you want to know what war is like, you have to watch this film and read other books, and maybe, maybe collectively, we'll say, ‘Enough.’" WATCH: 'Friday Night Lights' author Buzz Bissinger says 'The Mosquito Bowl' cast nailed it 'to a T' Bissinger told Fox News Digital that he keeps a picture of Schreiner hanging on his wall to remind him of the harsh realities of war and the sacrifices made by the fallen players. "I still can't quite comprehend that these guys are no longer with us," he said. "Dave Schreiner, beautiful guy, 6'2", perfect, the perfect two-time All-American, great son, great family, and his whole life ahead of him. And he died 12 hours before officials surrendered." "And I'm just haunted by that," Bissinger continued. "Because he should have — they should have had a life. They didn't waste their lives, but it's still, in a sense, is the waste of a good human being. And that's just hard for me to overcome. So he reminds me, he keeps me going." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE Bissinger admitted that ahead of watching "The Mosquito Bowl," he was worried about whether the film and its young cast would preserve the integrity of the men they were portraying. However, he told Fox News Digital that he was blown away by their performances. "They did it to a T," he said. "They're all great. Ray Nicholson will knock your socks off. Bill Skarsgård, Tom Francis, Nick Galitzine — they were phenomenal. And so at a certain point, I'm not looking at them as people they're making a movie about, I am seeing them now as the characters they were, and that was great." "The Mosquito Bowl" marks a creative reunion for Bissinger and Berg. The director previously adapted Bissinger's 1990 bestselling nonfiction book "Friday Night Lights" into the acclaimed 2004 movie of the same name and later the hit TV series that ran on NBC from 2006 to 2011. "We talk all the time. I pitch projects to him. He says, 'You're out of your mind. I'm not doing that.' But then something hits and it took a while. It took a little while." articles.title: Paralympian Ezra Frech is crowned ‘Dancing With the Stars’ winner
articles.summary: After weeks of rehearsals, heartwarming moments and dynamic dances, Ezra Frech was crowned the winner in the emotional finale of “Dancing with the Stars.”
articles.body: After weeks of rehearsals, heartwarming moments and dynamic dances, one celebrity was crowned the winner in the emotional three-hour finale of “Dancing With the Stars” on Tuesday. The winner of the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy for “DWTS” Season 35 was Paralympian Ezra Frech and his dancing partner Daniella Karagach. The two were in tears as their names were announced. Season 34 champs Robert Irwin and Witney Carson handed the trophy to the new winners. “This is the most special moment of my life,” said Frech, the first Paralympian to win “DWTS,” as he thanked fans for their votes. Karagach, who is now a two-time champ, added, “I’m just so freaking grateful.” Frech is a track star who competed at the 2024 Paris Paralympic Games, winning gold medals in both the 100 meter and high jump. He competes in the long jump, as well, and was the youngest member of the U.S. Paralympic team at the 2020 Tokyo Paralympic Games at just 16 years old. The finalists competing for the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy were Frech, Connor Wood, Amber Glenn, Tatyana Ali and Maura Higgins. The rest of the rankings: 2nd Place: Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov 3rd Place: Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold 4th Place: Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik 5th Place: Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas Before their first dance of the night, Frech and Karagach reflected on their journey throughout the competition. Judge Bruno Tonioli sat in on their rehearsal and revealed the two were dancing the salsa for their Judges’ Choice routine. He told Frech that he needed to work on his hip movement, and explained the need to move in a figure eight formation. Frech’s hips did not lie when the music to “Danza Kuduro” by Don Omar featuring Lucenzo began. He and Karagach delivered a spicy routine that had the audience on their feet by the end. Tonioli said Frech was possessed by “the devil of salsa” and brought a party to the dance floor. Judge Carrie Ann Inaba said what has been so impressive about Frech and Karagach’s pairing is how they dance in unison constantly. Judge Derek Hough said Frech’s risks paid off and he broke the mold with his salsa. The routine got a perfect 30 out of 30 from the judges. For the Instant Dance Challenge, Frech selected the tango, which he previously performed during the season premiere. He and Karagach prepared for the dance, set to “Levels” by Avicii, while viewers saw how the two came up with a strategy in their rehearsal days earlier. The pair learned each style and practiced them to different tempos. But, Frech shared that he preferred to dance the tango. His wish came true and resulted in a fiery routine. Tonioli said Frech was a “man on a mission” as he channeled a “strong, moody and aggressive” lover. Inaba said he has developed “artistry” since the first week of the competition. Hough said he was thankful Frech has educated people on what’s possible in dance. Frech and Karagach again scored a perfect 30 out of 30. Frech said he wanted his freestyle to be “a celebration of what is possible when you’re different.” He also told Karagach that being on the show has been “one of the most special journeys of my life” as he started to cry. He said he was grateful that Kragach wanted to highlight his prosthetic in every dance. They said they loved each other before hugging. For their routine, the two brought in wheelchair dancers. “To be the first ever amputee to win the Mirrorball would be a dream come true,” Frech said. He said he wanted to go all out to win it all. He did just that with a powerful freestyle set to “Numb” by Linkin Park. He began the dance without his prosthetic before putting it on. But, it briefly fell off. He stayed calm as Karagach helped him place it back on. Frech was fired up as the wheelchair dancers joined him. Karagach was in tears as the two received feedback from the judges. “Ezra, you are a hero,” Derek Hough praised. “This performance will have a ripple effect far beyond this show.” He added that kids will look up to him. Tonioli agreed it was a “powerful” moment that “goes beyond dancing.” Inabe applauded Karagach’s routine before complimenting Frech for delivering his “purpose” every time he stepped on the ballroom floor. Frech told judge Julianne Hough that the two put their hearts, blood, sweat and tears into the performance. He also said he did his job if he made one person with a disability feel more confident. The freestyle also scored a perfect 30, with the duo racking up a final score of 90 out of 90.

articles.title: Christina Ricci admits Cher is 'still mad at me' decades after one mistake ended 'Mermaids' bond
articles.summary: Christina Ricci says Cher still holds a grudge over a voicemail she never returned at 19, decades after they played mother and daughter in "Mermaids."
articles.body: Nearly four decades after playing mother and daughter in the 1990 classic "Mermaids," Christina Ricci revealed that her off-screen relationship with Cher has been rocky — all because of an unreturned voicemail from when Ricci was 19. During a recent appearance on "Watch What Happens Live," host Andy Cohen asked Ricci if she had stayed in touch with the music icon after filming "Mermaids" and appearing in the video for "The Shoop Shoop Song." "I’m not," Ricci admitted. "Unfortunately, she's still mad at me. She holds a grudge." According to the "Yellowjackets" star, the rift dates back to a magazine interview in which Cher made remarks about Ricci that "were not that amazing." Realizing how the quotes came across, Cher called Ricci to smooth things over. CHRISTINA RICCI WILL NEVER BE 'GIRL NEXT DOOR,' SAYS HAPPY PEOPLE DON'T DO ANYTHING INTERESTING "She left me a voicemail about how journalists are always trying to get the worst things, and blah blah blah," Ricci recalled. "And she was so sorry, and I was 19, and so I didn't return that message." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE That teenage oversight appears to have stuck. Ricci noted that her efforts to reconnect with Cher over the years have been met with "radio silence." Despite the decades-long silent treatment, Ricci holds no ill will — and even took Cher's side in the standoff, noting how supportive the Oscar winner had been to her as a child actor on set. "And I absolutely can 100 percent imagine being Cher and being like, 'Oh, my God, they misquoted me, and I'm going to call this young person and explain to her that they misquoted me.' And then the gall of that young person to not return the call and be like, 'Oh, my God, Cher, it's OK. I love you so much.' Like, I would be so pissed. I get it." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS In one last effort, Ricci looked straight into the camera to offer a direct, public olive branch: "Love you, Cher. I love you so much." Released in December 1990, the 1960s-set comedy-drama served as Ricci’s big-screen debut, casting the then-9-year-old newcomer as Kate Flax, the swim-obsessed youngest daughter of Cher’s free-spirited single mom, Rachel, alongside Winona Ryder. The film was a major cultural moment for the trio, even spawning Cher’s chart-topping cover of "The Shoop Shoop Song (It's in His Kiss)," whose iconic music video featured both Ryder and Ricci. articles.title: John F Kennedy Jr search commander says Ted Kennedy made one strict demand after divers found nephew’s body
articles.summary: New book "The Last Flight" details the 1999 search off Martha's Vineyard where John F. Kennedy Jr.'s body was recovered with his wife and her sister.
articles.body: In the agonizing days following the 1999 plane crash that killed John F. Kennedy Jr., his wife Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and her sister Lauren Bessette, Sen. Ted Kennedy issued a strict, emotional mandate to the federal crews racing to recover their bodies: All three would be brought to the surface together. Retired U.S. Coast Guard Capt. W. Russell Webster, who spearheaded the search efforts, co-wrote "The Last Flight" with his wife, maritime historian Theresa Mitchell Webster. The book chronicles the massive recovery mission after Kennedy's single-engine plane crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off Martha's Vineyard. Navy divers recovered all three bodies on July 21, 1999 — five days after the plane went down off Martha's Vineyard. LAST PERSON TO SEE JFK JR. ALIVE REVEALS CHILLING PREMONITION ABOUT HIS FATAL FLIGHT THAT NIGHT "It became more complicated to ensure that his family's wishes were followed," Webster told Fox News Digital about the senator. "It was complicated because, normally, when bodies are recovered, they're recovered individually. He insisted that his nephew not be recovered as a priority. That was difficult, not only during the later body recovery, but also very early on when John F. Kennedy Jr. was found outside the airplane." Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links. "There was a sense of urgency, driven primarily by the family doctor to have the divers go back down and retrieve him," said Webster. In the book, Webster wrote, "Senator Kennedy was adamant that Navy divers bring up John, Carolyn and Lauren at the exact same time in a single salvage basket. Even though his staffers initially pushed for JFK Jr. to be raised first because his body was outside the wreckage while the women were trapped inside, the senator insisted they be recovered together, so his nephew would not be perceived as receiving special treatment, even in death." WATCH: JOHN F. KENNEDY JR. RECOVERY COMMANDER RECOUNTS 5-DAY SEARCH MISSION Webster wrote that the divers were racing against time. "Walking the Atlantic floor stirs up silt, further compromising low visibility," he wrote. The divers quickly found Kennedy's Piper Saratoga. There was no roof on the plane, and the windows were missing, "having been blown out from the impact." Kennedy Jr. was on his side on the ocean floor near the wreckage. "Senator Kennedy insisted that the bodies be raised together at the same time," Mitchell Webster told Fox News Digital. "So, the Navy on the USS Grasp, has what's called a basket. It's a large metal piece with sides for the divers to hang onto. The platform on which they stood in that basket was large enough for them to put three bodies on it. So, they were raised together, and no preferential treatment was shown to JFK Jr." "His uncle, from what we've been told and from what Russ had observed, was extremely respectful of the process and extremely grateful, as was his family, to the people doing the work." The Bessette sisters were found together inside the upside-down fuselage, still strapped into their seats. The book describes Kennedy as a constant, protective presence who remained beside his nephew and the Bessette sisters. Once the remains were transferred onto a 55-foot Coast Guard vessel, Kennedy and his sons boarded with them. During the transit, with a Navy chaplain in attendance, the senator invited the Coast Guard crew to join his family in prayer. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE When the boat reached shore, Kennedy overruled an aide who wanted to delay unloading until more relatives arrived. He insisted the caskets be brought straight to the waiting hearses. He stepped in to help carry them. "He obviously never left their sides," said Webster. "After everything was done, he and his wife visited my command at Woods Hole and recognized everybody. He took pictures with everybody, gave out cookies and brownies. It was a very human experience." In retrieving the bodies, the crew wasn't just worried about beating the elements. There were also potential looters. Webster said they were driven by a very real fear that "treasure hunters" or commercial fishermen would stumble upon the wreckage first and steal personal items to profit off the tragedy. "I think it certainly was a motivation, the potential for not only treasure hunters, but also for fishermen," said Webster. "This was an active fishing area, and we knew we were driven by the fact, not only by the priority given to us, but also with the knowledge that leaving the wreckage and leaving the victims behind was an unacceptable outcome." It was one fisherman in those active waters who unknowingly became a key witness to the tragedy. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Just before 9:40 p.m. on July 16, 1999, Pittsburgh attorney Victor Pribanic was casting his line for striped bass off Squibnocket Point on the southwestern tip of Martha's Vineyard. A loud, jarring sound echoed across the dark Atlantic. He turned toward the open ocean, saw nothing in the haze and went back to fishing. Pribanic was unaware that he had just heard the final moments of Kennedy's plane. "It wasn't an explosion. It was a boom," said Webster. "The impact was grave, and it was severe. They likely just went down 116 feet." Looking back, Webster said he was proud of his crew's commitment to duty in retrieving Kennedy's beloved nephew and his family, even as a heavy sadness settled over everyone involved. "I remember feeling exhaustion," said Webster. "I believe I had just laid down for no more than an hour after not sleeping since I got the original call. It was a mixed feeling, a feeling of profound grief and a feeling of profound happiness. "I worked with a number of families that we could never save their loved ones or find their remains so that they could celebrate their lives in ceremonies. For me, it was a dichotomy of feelings. One was, 'Oh my God, we found them as a team.' And the other was, 'Yes, they're really dead.'" WATCH: AVIATION EXPERT EXPLAINS JFK JR.'S FINAL FLIGHT RISKS Ultimately, the National Transportation Safety Board determined the crash was caused by spatial disorientation. Though Kennedy Jr. had recently passed his written instrument exam, he was not yet certified to fly solely using his cockpit instruments. Just weeks before the crash, a certified flight instructor had noted in his record that he was not ready for instrument conditions. "What was clear to me was that in those final miles, he had transitioned into an instrument-rated flight that he was not prepared for," Webster said. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Even for fully qualified pilots, it can take up to 35 seconds to recover from spatial disorientation, Webster said. It’s a critical window Kennedy Jr. didn't have once the plane began its steep descent. "He had to have been anguished, confused, just frightened," said Mitchell Webster. "It must have been very difficult." On July 22, 1999, the families scattered the ashes of Kennedy Jr. and the Bessette sisters in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Martha's Vineyard. articles.title: Morgan Freeman’s grandchildren enter emergency housing after adviser rejects mother’s $5,000 plea for rent help; she says $100,000 divorce settlement could secure a home
articles.summary: Morgan Freeman’s three grandchildren have moved into emergency housing after their mother, Maryann Castle, says she was unable to keep up with rent and
articles.body: Morgan Freeman’s three grandchildren have moved into emergency housing after their mother, Maryann Castle, says she was unable to keep up with rent and received no financial assistance following repeated appeals to the actor. Castle, 48, says she asked Freeman for $5,000 to help prevent another eviction, but his business adviser told her the actor would not be able to assist.In an interview with the Daily Mail, Castle said she was trying to secure a safe and stable home for her children: Zaharah, six, Aaliyaah, eight, and Abdullah, 14. The family had previously fled their home in Michigan following what Castle describes as years of physical, mental and verbal abuse by Freeman’s son, Saifoulaye Freeman.The children and their mother are now staying in emergency accommodation, with a local nonprofit covering their rent. However, Castle says the arrangement is temporary and that they have around four months to find somewhere permanent.Mother says Morgan Freeman’s adviser declined her requestCastle told the Daily Mail that she repeatedly contacted the Oscar-winning actor for financial help after falling behind on rent. She said she requested $5,000, but received a response from his business adviser stating that Freeman could not assist her.The newspaper said it had seen emails Castle sent to the actor and his New York-based business adviser. In one message from July 2024, Castle told Freeman that she and the children had fled his son and stayed at a domestic violence shelter. She later wrote that they had found a home but needed help furnishing it.In an October email, she asked the adviser to pass on her request, explaining that the family was a week away from eviction. When she subsequently asked whether Freeman had received her messages, the adviser reportedly replied: “Morgan received all your messages. There is nothing he would do at this time.”Castle said the response left her feeling that the actor did not care about the children. She told the newspaper that her priority was to ensure they had a safe and secure home.A representative for Freeman told the Daily Mail that the actor does not discuss family matters publicly.Castle says she fled with her children in November 2023Castle claims she left the family home in Coopersville, Michigan, on November 3, 2023, after years of alleged abuse by Saifoulaye, now 65. She said she had only two days to plan the escape and enlisted the help of one of her stepsons and her adult son from a previous relationship.According to Castle, she waited until Saifoulaye left for dialysis treatment before waking the younger children. She said she and her older sons packed clothes, blankets and the children’s tablets into three suitcases before switching off security cameras that she alleges her former husband had installed inside the house.Castle told the newspaper that Saifoulaye discovered the cameras had been turned off and returned home, leaving the family with around 15 minutes to get away. She said they decided not to return, even after she realised she had left her driving licence behind.The family spent seven months in a domestic violence shelter before moving into a home with help from an abuse charity, which supported their rent for two years. That assistance has since ended.Court judgment shows family faced evictionAccording to a court judgment obtained by the Daily Mail, Castle was required to pay more than $6,500 by November 30 to remain in the property. Unable to raise the amount, she and the children moved into emergency accommodation, where a local nonprofit is covering their rent.Castle, who says she is the children’s sole carer, also told the newspaper that two of them have autism and ADHD. She said she and the children have experienced post-traumatic stress following the alleged abuse and have received therapy.The family’s longer-term housing situation remains uncertain. Castle said the emergency accommodation is available for only four months, after which they may have to move into her mother’s one-bedroom cabin, more than an hour away. Such a move could also mean the children having to change schools.Protection order and allegations of abuseCastle and Saifoulaye began their relationship in 2003 after meeting in an online chatroom. They married in November 2011. She alleges that abusive behaviour began early in their relationship, describing incidents involving intimidation and violence.In December 2023, Castle obtained a personal protection order (PPO) covering herself and the children. A copy of the order, obtained by the Daily Mail, shows that Saifoulaye opposed it. The order expired in December 2024.In her application, Castle alleged that Saifoulaye had repeatedly threatened to kill her if she left him. She also described an alleged 2012 incident in which he punched her in the head and threatened her with a stair stepper. In another account, she alleged that he shook her by the shoulders shortly before she fled and threatened to destroy her electronic devices.Castle further alleged that he monitored her through the home security cameras and used religious rules to restrict her movements. These are allegations made by Castle in her account and protection-order application.The Daily Mail also reported that Saifoulaye pleaded guilty to third-degree child abuse in July 2006 after beating his then 10-year-old son, Hussein, with a belt. A sentencing document obtained by the newspaper said the boy suffered significant bruising and cuts. The filings also alleged that the belt had been used on other children in the household.Castle said Hussein died by suicide in December 2014 and believed he had struggled with his relationships with his biological parents.Divorce settlement remains a key part of the disputeCastle and Saifoulaye divorced in July 2024. She told the Daily Mail that their divorce agreement requires him to pay her $100,000 within two years or sell their former marital home and give her half the proceeds.Castle alleges that Saifoulaye has told her he will not sell the property or pay the amount. She said the money would help her and the children secure a permanent home.The newspaper reported that the former family home appeared to be in poor condition when its reporters visited. No one answered the door, although the lights were on. A neighbour reportedly said groceries had been delivered recently but that they had not seen anyone coming or going for some time.Castle says Freeman knows about his grandchildrenCastle said Morgan Freeman is aware of the three children’s existence, although she claims he has never met them. She said the actor had met some of Saifoulaye’s older children during a family gathering in Chicago and had also met her adult son, Khaleed, in California last year.She further claimed that the younger children are included in the Morgan Freeman Trust and that the family receives annual letters about payments into it. However, Castle said the actor’s adviser told her that no money could be withdrawn from the trust at present.For now, she says, the prospect of a future inheritance does little to address the family’s immediate housing needs.In a direct appeal to Freeman, Castle said she wanted him to speak to his son and encourage him to honour the divorce settlement so that she and the children could buy a home.“The kids and I really need your help,” she told the Daily Mail. “What I'm trying to do is get me and the kids into a house that is permanent, so that we don't have to move again.”Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.summary: Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez recall their "toxic and at times dangerous" teen rivalry on Sheen's "Mostly Sheenius" podcast, and a high school fight.

During a recent appearance on Sheen’s "Mostly Sheenius" podcast, the brothers reminisced about their "toxic" and "dangerous" teenage rivalry. "We didn't always get along.
